title: Malpractice insurance: Reported AI claims remain hard to isolate
desc: Places emerging claims within broader loss trends and disputed coverage, where sanctions and insurer concern do not measure incidence.

kps.k: AI malpractice has entered reported claims experience, but its incidence and contribution to rising losses remain uncertain.
kps.d: Ames & Gough’s 2024 survey found only one insurer had encountered an AI-related malpractice claim; EPIC’s 2025 announcement reported concern without quantifying AI claims. EPIC’s 2026 survey then found seven of 13 insurers reporting increases over the preceding year. These are insurer observations, not claim counts or exposure-adjusted rates. The repeated accounts of EPIC’s announcement do not supply independent corroboration, and the supplied material lacks the full survey. Browning notes that confidential settlements obscure totals, while Business Insurance’s interviewees still describe limited claims. The actuary.info article advances a structural-shift interpretation but explicitly leaves AI’s role in the overall frequency increase unresolved.

qs.q: Meanwhile, despite  AI being a top line concern for the majority of the insurers we polled, only  one insurer had seen an AI related legal malpractice claim whereas all of the  insurers have seen an increase in cyber related legal malpractice claims.
qs.a: Law Firms Navigate Unrelenting Challenges of Lateral Movement, Cyber Threats, AI Risks and Fraud — Ames & Gough 2024 LPLI Claims Survey (14th annual) · Liability insurers · 2024

qs.q: Seven of the 13 insurers polled said they had seen an increase in AI-related claims in the last year.
qs.a: EPIC Insurance Brokers & Consultants Reports First Rise in Legal Malpractice Claims in Five Years · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: AI exposure sits within a broader malpractice market already facing severe losses and rising defense costs.
kps.d: EPIC’s 2026 survey reports higher overall frequency at eight of 13 insurers, materially higher defense spending at eleven, and planned rate increases at a majority. These findings do not isolate AI’s contribution. Conflicts and complex transactional work remain central exposures; earlier Ames & Gough findings already documented nine-figure payouts. Bovitz’s comparison further distinguishes routine claims from catastrophic losses associated with problematic clients and cautions that study populations differ substantially. The practical implication is to add AI controls without displacing established conflict checks, client intake, supervision and payment-security safeguards.

qs.q: **Rising Defense Costs Pressure the Market**  Meanwhile, the cost of defending malpractice claims continues to increase, with 11 of 13 insurers polled reporting materially higher defense spending year over year.
qs.a: EPIC Insurance Brokers & Consultants Reports First Rise in Legal Malpractice Claims in Five Years · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: A majority of surveyed insurers indicated plans to raise rates in 2026.
qs.a: EPIC Insurance Brokers & Consultants Reports First Rise in Legal Malpractice Claims in Five Years · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Court sanctions demonstrate misconduct, not insured malpractice losses, and insurance generally does not reimburse punishment.
kps.d: Browning, Spears and Business Insurance use fabricated-citation incidents to illustrate failures to check AI output. They distinguish sanctions from subsequent client claims and disciplinary proceedings. Browning explains that professional liability insurance may fund negligence defense and indemnity, and limited disciplinary defense, while generally excluding court sanctions. The actuary.info article argues that sanctions can precede follow-on malpractice claims and unusually expensive parallel proceedings; its proposed six-to-eighteen-month lag and cost estimates remain attributed assessments, not established market-wide loss-development patterns. Sanctions databases therefore cannot substitute for malpractice claims data or model error-rate measurements.

qs.q: First of all, court-ordered sanctions are generally not covered under typical LPL policies.
qs.a: AI and Legal Malpractice: Are We Due for a Reckoning? · Academia · 2026

qs.q: But direct sanctions understate the total exposure because each incident can generate multiple follow-on claims: a malpractice suit from the affected client, disciplinary proceedings from the state bar, and reputational harm that compounds across a firm's entire book of business.
qs.a: Legal Malpractice Carriers Face First Wave of AI Claims as LPL Coverage Forms Outpace the Cyber Cycle · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The central coverage disagreement concerns whether unchecked AI use remains ordinary insured negligence.
kps.d: Business Insurance’s specialists generally treat AI errors like other professional mistakes, covered unless excluded. Lockton reaches a similar conclusion for solicitors subject to SRA minimum terms, a distinct jurisdictional basis. By contrast, Bassingthwaighte, Burke and Bennett warn that extreme blind reliance could fall outside a policy’s definition of professional services; Bassingthwaighte also raises intentional-act exclusions. These warnings propose possible insurer arguments, not adjudicated denials. Bassingthwaighte separately identifies jurisdiction-dependent unauthorized-practice and professional-services issues when client-facing AI makes critical legal judgments without lawyer oversight. Neither a blanket assurance of coverage nor a blanket assumption of exclusion captures these positions.

qs.q: Most E&O and cyber liability policies are written broadly enough to cover errors in professional services or security and privacy failures, regardless of the technology involved, unless they include a specific AI exclusion, said Kara Higginbotham, New York-based head of professional liability and cyber at Zurich North America.
qs.a: AI use amplifies professional liability risks (with sidebar: Insurers cautious on E&O exclusions) · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: PII policies should therefore respond where AI is used to perform legal duties and a claim against the insured later arises in relation to an alleged breach of those duties.
qs.a: Law firm AI: insurance considerations · Liability insurers · 2024

kps.k: Exclusions and affirmative AI products coexist, making policy wording more informative than broad claims about market direction.
kps.d: Browning reports absolute exclusions, naming Berkley Select, whereas the actuary.info article reports no explicit exclusion on major US writers’ named LPL forms as of May 2026 and places most restrictions in other liability lines. The supplied accounts do not resolve this tension across carriers, forms and dates. Other reporting identifies tailored Munich Re and Armilla products and a sublimited Markel miscellaneous E&O endorsement—not uniform law-firm coverage. Braff and Buchanan recommend scrutinizing definitions, exclusions, sublimits and individually negotiated wording. Firms must also distinguish professional liability from cyber, management, employment and performance-warranty coverage; a dedicated AI or cyber policy does not necessarily fill every gap.

qs.q: A number of carriers, such as Berkley Select, have publicly announced “absolute” exclusions for AI use.
qs.a: AI and Legal Malpractice: Are We Due for a Reckoning? · Academia · 2026

qs.q: LPL writer (CNA, Travelers, Chubb, Hartford, Markel, ALPS, or state mutuals) has filed an explicit AI exclusion on its named lawyers' professional liability form.
qs.a: Legal Malpractice Carriers Face First Wave of AI Claims as LPL Coverage Forms Outpace the Cyber Cycle · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Insurance underwriting may turn AI governance into a commercial requirement, but its pricing effects remain largely predictive.
kps.d: The actuary.info article reports renewal questions about tools, written policies, training, human verification and incident response. Burke describes inquiries in March 2026 as largely preliminary and predicts that firms without documented protocols will lose preferred terms over the next 12–18 months. Business Insurance highlights embedded AI and unapproved use as obstacles to understanding exposure. Across these accounts, recommendations converge on tool inventories, task-appropriate selection, vendor diligence, verification records, supervision, privacy safeguards and client communication. Browning predicts that threatened coverage will improve vigilance; neither that behavioral effect nor a quantified governance-related reduction in losses is demonstrated.

qs.q: CNA's supplemental AI questionnaire covers five core areas: which AI tools the firm uses, whether a written AI governance policy exists, whether attorneys receive AI-specific training, how AI-generated work product is reviewed and verified, and whether the firm has an AI incident response plan.
qs.a: Legal Malpractice Carriers Face First Wave of AI Claims as LPL Coverage Forms Outpace the Cyber Cycle · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: “For now, it remains largely a check-the-box inquiry as underwriters continue to monitor how AI adoption evolves.”  Burke recommends that law firms implement AI governance frameworks that define permissible use and verification standards while ensuring audit trails of AI-generated content are maintained.
qs.a: How Generative AI Is Reshaping Professional Liability Risk for Law Firms · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Immature loss histories constrain actuarial pricing and reserving even as insurers respond to emerging exposure.
kps.d: The actuary.info article identifies insufficient loss-development data, changing model failure mechanisms and heterogeneous coverage as obstacles to conventional pricing. It reports reliance on analogous risks and underwriting judgment, including judgment-based AI endorsement surcharges, and predicts that pre-2023 development assumptions may understate ultimate 2024–2025 losses. These are reserve-adequacy warnings, not measured shortfalls. Business Insurance adds that competitive pressures can restrain exclusions. The practical question is how to update rates and reserves as credible experience accumulates, without treating sanctions counts, broader AI litigation or forecasts from other professions as legal-malpractice loss evidence.

qs.q: **No historical loss development data.** AI-related legal malpractice claims are too new to have credible loss triangles.
qs.a: Legal Malpractice Carriers Face First Wave of AI Claims as LPL Coverage Forms Outpace the Cyber Cycle · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: # Insurers cautious on E&O exclusions  Competitive pressures are influencing insurers’ decisions to make restrictive changes to policy wording, sources say.
qs.a: AI use amplifies professional liability risks (with sidebar: Insurers cautious on E&O exclusions) · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The prevailing practical proposition favors controlled adoption, not AI avoidance or transfer of professional responsibility to technology.
kps.d: Ames & Gough and Lockton acknowledge potential efficiency and error-reduction benefits while recommending measured adoption. Browning argues that competence includes understanding benefits and reports conditional views that non-use could eventually create duty-of-care or fee disputes; these are not settled duties to adopt AI. The Billable Hour Death Spiral separately warns that billing unchanged amounts after AI compresses work could invite fee-reasonableness scrutiny. Embroker presents insurance as enabling innovation, but its voluntary survey measures confidence rather than verified protection: 77% believed their policies covered their greatest risks. The resulting tension is between enabling useful adoption and preserving human judgment, defensible fees and actual coverage.

qs.q: Most insurers view AI as a benefit to the legal industry based on its ability to  save time and reduce costs while cutting down on errors.
qs.a: Law Firms Navigate Unrelenting Challenges of Lateral Movement, Cyber Threats, AI Risks and Fraud — Ames & Gough 2024 LPLI Claims Survey (14th annual) · Liability insurers · 2024

qs.q: Insurers recognise that a sensible approach for law firms to take in adopting AI tools is to proceed with change while being aware of the risks and managing or mitigating them as far as possible.
qs.a: Law firm AI: insurance considerations · Liability insurers · 2024

vlens.an: These selected professional-body sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition that AI-related malpractice incidence remains uncertain and that coverage cannot be inferred from general market claims. They materially develop the proposition by explaining why policy-level scrutiny is necessary: malpractice, cyber and AI-specific products may differ in definitions, exclusions, sublimits and scope, while affirmative AI coverage is often individually negotiated following system-specific due diligence. Their common practical conclusion is that firms should verify actual wording and coordinate overlapping policies rather than assume either blanket coverage or blanket exclusion. There is some internal variation: the ABA Journal article adds concrete underwriting, vendor-risk and coverage-coordination considerations, whereas the Year 2 report emphasizes the lightly regulated surplus-lines setting and careful buyer review; its separate long-term discussion forecasts advanced AI but does not resolve malpractice-claim incidence. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: But “as with all policies, the devil is in the details of the specific terms and conditions of a policy to determine scope of coverage.”
qs.a: Does Your Professional Liability Insurance Cover AI Mistakes? Don't Be So Sure · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Businesses purchasing these novel insurance products should scrutinize their wordings carefully, with the help of counsel if necessary, to make sure that they unambiguously provide the scope of coverage promised and expected.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research evidence supports the cluster’s principal proposition. Browning accepts that AI-related malpractice claims have entered reported experience while stressing that confidential settlements and incomplete reporting prevent reliable incidence estimates. He also aligns with the synthesis by separating court sanctions from insured malpractice losses, describing both broad AI exclusions and affirmative AI products, and favouring controlled adoption with human vigilance rather than AI avoidance. Material variation lies within his argument rather than across academic sources: he is cautious about current claims evidence and acknowledges that broader increases in malpractice severity and defence costs do not isolate AI’s contribution, but he is more confident when predicting that threats to professional-liability coverage will improve lawyers’ conduct. That behavioural effect remains a forecast, not a demonstrated finding. Because the evidence contains only one curated academic source, this position should not be treated as representative of academia or research generally.

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analysis, consultancy and press sources supports the proposition that AI-related malpractice has entered reported insurer experience but cannot yet be isolated reliably from broader claims trends. Common reasons include the absence of claim counts and exposure-adjusted rates, limited and immature loss-development data, differences among study populations, and the need to distinguish court sanctions from insured malpractice losses. The sources also broadly agree that existing professional-liability coverage often extends to ordinary AI-related negligence unless policy wording excludes it, while extreme failures of verification, unsupervised client-facing tools, confidentiality breaches or intentional conduct may generate policy-specific coverage disputes. They converge practically on controlled adoption through human review, tool selection, documented governance and supervision, while treating governance-based pricing penalties and reserve inadequacy mainly as predictions rather than demonstrated market effects. Material internal variation concerns emphasis and confidence: EPIC and Bovitz place AI among established exposures such as conflicts, supervision failures and problematic clients; Business Insurance stresses that malpractice claims remain limited; Bassingthwaighte develops conditional noncoverage arguments; and the actuary.info article advances stronger forecasts about structural loss growth and reserve pressure while acknowledging that AI’s contribution to overall frequency remains unresolved. The Billable Hour Death Spiral extends the discussion toward fee reasonableness and human value, but does not supply incidence evidence. These positions describe only the supplied curated sources and should not be treated as representative of all analysts, consultancies or press coverage.

qs.q: Whether the AI claims component is driving the broader frequency increase or merely coinciding with it remains an open question, but the correlation is difficult to dismiss.
qs.a: Legal Malpractice Carriers Face First Wave of AI Claims as LPL Coverage Forms Outpace the Cyber Cycle · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: That said, coverage may depend on whether the conduct at issue meets the policy’s definition of “professional services.” Don’t assume that it always will.
qs.a: Insurance Coverage Issues for Lawyers in the Era of Generative AI · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The curated professional-liability-insurer sources support the proposition that AI-related malpractice exposure is emerging but remains difficult to isolate from broader claims trends. Their common reasoning is that insurer concern and reported increases do not themselves establish claim counts, exposure-adjusted incidence, or AI’s causal contribution to overall loss frequency and severity. They consistently place AI alongside established drivers such as conflicts, complex transactional work, cyber incidents, supervision failures, rising defense costs and social inflation. They also generally favour controlled adoption—training, supervision, governance, verification and appropriate insurance review—rather than avoidance or transferring professional responsibility to technology. Material variation is chiefly temporal and jurisdictional: Ames & Gough’s 2024 survey found only one insurer with an AI-related claim, EPIC’s 2025 release quantified concern but not incidents, and EPIC’s 2026 announcement reported seven of 13 insurers seeing increases. Lockton contributes a UK-specific view that SRA-compliant professional indemnity insurance should respond to alleged breaches involving AI, while also predicting greater disclosure and underwriting scrutiny; Ames & Gough is more cautious about placing AI and cyber losses within lawyers’ professional liability coverage. Embroker is the least direct claims evidence because its voluntary survey measures legal professionals’ perceived risks and confidence in insurance rather than insurer loss experience or verified coverage. These selected sources therefore reinforce both the emergence of the exposure and the synthesis’s evidentiary and coverage cautions, without showing how representative these positions are of professional-liability insurers generally.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that reported AI-related malpractice claims were difficult to isolate from broader loss trends and that insurer concern was running ahead of demonstrated claims experience. Ames & Gough supplies the period’s clearest empirical support: among its 13 participating insurers, only one had encountered an AI-related legal-malpractice claim, even though AI was a leading concern. At the same time, it reports severe losses, rising defence costs and established exposures such as conflicts and drafting errors, so the broader malpractice deterioration cannot be attributed to AI. Lockton supports the proposition’s coverage and governance dimensions rather than independently establishing claim incidence. Under the UK SRA framework, it expects professional indemnity insurance generally to respond when AI is used in performing legal duties, while treating increased disclosure, underwriting questions and warranties largely as prospective developments. Both sources favour controlled adoption with supervision and risk mitigation, not AI avoidance. Material internal variation lies in emphasis and jurisdiction: Ames & Gough reports US insurer experience and also states that insurers do not want AI and cyber losses falling under lawyers’ professional liability policies, whereas Lockton reasons that UK solicitors’ PII should respond to claims alleging breach of AI-assisted legal duties. This is a genuine difference in coverage framing, but not opposition to the principal proposition; it reinforces the synthesis’s warning against blanket coverage claims. These two curated sources should not be treated as representative of all insurers, brokers or jurisdictions.

qs.q: Meanwhile, despite  AI being a top line concern for the majority of the insurers we polled, only  one insurer had seen an AI related legal malpractice claim whereas all of the  insurers have seen an increase in cyber related legal malpractice claims.

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that AI-related malpractice exposure is emerging but remains difficult to isolate from broader claims and cost trends. Insurer reporting identifies AI as a concern alongside attorney oversight and cyber risk, yet supplies neither AI-specific claim counts nor exposure-adjusted incidence; other 2025 evidence likewise consists largely of voluntary survey perceptions, advisory analysis and market examples rather than verified loss outcomes. The sources materially extend the proposition by detailing why coverage cannot be inferred categorically: professional-services definitions, intentional-act and unauthorized-practice exclusions, cyber-policy variation, sublimits, individualized due diligence and bespoke affirmative AI products can all affect whether a loss is insured. They also converge on controlled adoption through verification, lawyer supervision, privacy safeguards, vendor scrutiny and written governance rather than AI avoidance. Material internal variation concerns emphasis and evidentiary basis: Bovitz and EPIC situate AI within established malpractice drivers and rising defense costs; Braff, Bassingthwaighte and Buchanan focus on conditional policy wording and possible coverage gaps; Embroker presents governance and insurance confidence as enabling adoption, although its voluntary survey measures beliefs and concerns rather than claims or verified protection; and the long-term-future section redirects some attention toward speculative advanced-AI preparation without contradicting the insurance proposition. These relationships describe only the supplied curated sources and do not establish how prevalent any view was among insurers, lawyers or firms in 2025.

qs.q: When asked about specific issues keeping them up at night, the surveyed insurers named cyber and attorney oversight as top areas of concern, as well as AI risks.
qs.a: EPIC Law Firm Group Releases Key Trends Driving Law Firm Malpractice Insurance Claims in Annual Survey — 15th annual Lawyers' Professional Liability Claims Survey · Liability insurers · 2025

elens.an:
The curated 2026 sources support the proposition that AI-related malpractice has entered reported insurer experience but remains difficult to isolate, quantify and price. Their common basis is cautious separation of evidence from inference: EPIC reports that insurers observed increases in AI-related claims, yet supplies neither claim counts nor exposure-adjusted rates; other sources note confidential settlements, still-limited claims experience and immature actuarial histories. They also place AI within a wider malpractice market shaped by conflicts, complex transactional work, severe losses and rising defense costs, so the broader deterioration cannot be attributed to AI alone. The repeated accounts of EPIC’s announcement are not independent corroboration.

The sources further agree that sanctions for fabricated citations illustrate verification failures but are not themselves insured malpractice losses, and that human oversight, documented governance and task-appropriate tools are central controls. Material variation concerns coverage and market response. Some industry specialists generally treat AI-caused negligence as covered under existing policies unless expressly excluded; others suggest that extreme blind reliance might fall outside covered professional services. Sources report both exclusions and affirmative AI products, making policy-specific wording decisive. They also differ in evidential strength: current underwriting questionnaires and governance scrutiny are reported developments, whereas loss of preferred terms, reserve inadequacy, structural claims growth and insurance-driven behavioural change remain predictions. The billing-focused source extends the practical discussion to fee reasonableness and human judgment without displacing the principal malpractice-insurance proposition. This alignment describes only the supplied curated sources and does not establish prevalence among insurers, brokers, actuaries or legal professionals generally.
